\begin{abstract}
Does mandated climate adaptation pay for itself? I study a 1994 wind standard reform that required structural upgrades to manufactured homes in hurricane-prone areas. The estimated resale price premium is roughly `r tex(cl_premium_2_pct)` in the most exposed counties, but is imprecisely estimated. However, surviving quantities in those counties fall by up to `r tex(cl_count_drop_z3)`, implying that the cost of the wind standard exceeded the private value buyers placed on it. I support this conclusion using claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program, where I compare flood damage to manufactured and site-built homes of different construction vintages exposed to floods in the same county and over the same period. The pooled estimate indicates a `r tex(bldg_dmg_pct)` reduction in building damage per claim for post-1994 manufactured homes relative to site-built homes, although event-study and triple-difference estimates are imprecise. The present value of these benefits is small -- only `r cl_flood_pv` per insured home -- reflecting the low baseline values of insured manufactured homes. For manufactured-home owners, mandatory climate adaptation does not generally pay for itself.
\end{abstract}

\begin{quotation}\small
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} climate adaptation, building codes, manufactured housing, hurricane risk, flood insurance, housing prices
\end{quotation}

# Introduction

The U.S. experienced more than 100 billion-dollar climate disasters in the five years before 2026, with damages exceeding \$600 billion.[^billion-dollar] These costs are projected to grow substantially as climate change intensifies extreme weather events. Building codes and other forms of mandated adaptation investment are a potential policy tool for reducing disaster losses and risk, but the returns to these investments, and how those returns vary across housing types, are not well understood. This paper provides new evidence on the costs and benefits of mandated adaptation in the context of manufactured housing (MH), a sector that is both highly vulnerable to climate risk and largely uninsured.[^mh]

[^billion-dollar]: Climate Central. "U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters." ClimateCentral.Org, 2026. \href{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}.

[^mh]: "Manufactured homes" are the preferred industry term and refer specifically to mobile homes that satisfy the 1976 HUD Code. Because the vast majority of mobile homes produced since 1976 satisfy the code, I use the terms "manufactured" and "mobile" interchangeably.

Government mandates for costly adaptation may be justified if private take-up is hindered by frictions. For instance, households may misperceive climate risk [@bakkensen_going_2022; @gallagher_learning_2014]. They may fail to internalize benefits to their neighbors [@baylis_mandated_2026]. They may enjoy limited upside from adaptation if mitigation behaviors are not reflected in insurance premiums [@wagner_adaptation_2022]. Finally, they may rely on public insurance programs and disaster relief instead [@deryugina_fiscal_2017; @baylis_moral_2019].

However, mandated adaptation can be costly. Households may prefer to limit their exposure to climate risks by buying a less expensive home, limiting both their potential losses and the benefits of investments in adaptation [@grames_optimal_2019; @castro-vincenzi_climate_2022]. If adaptation involves fixed costs, or costs that do not move proportionally with home value, it may be unattractive to households with low-value homes.

I examine this question using a federal 1994 reform to building codes for manufactured homes. To guide the empirical approach, I use two key results from a basic theoretical framework. First, the value that the marginal household places on the additional climate protection is reflected in the difference in market prices between homes built before and after the reform. That is, the reform's benefits are fully capitalized into the resale price of treated homes. I estimate this price gap using a difference-in-differences design, comparing manufactured-home prices across construction vintages and wind zones. I also use site-built homes as an additional comparison group in a triple-difference specification. The design exploits the fact that only manufactured homes built after 1994 in high-wind zones were subject to the reform. I find suggestive evidence that buyers value the additional resilience. The estimated premium is about `r cl_premium_2_pct` of the resale price, or `r cl_premium` per home, but is not statistically significant at conventional levels.

Second, a sufficient statistic for the net private benefit of the reform is its effect on the quantity of newly placed MH [@summers_simple_1989]. Intuitively, if buyers value the reform by more than the associated cost, they will demand at least as many new MH as they would have absent the reform. Conversely, if private valuations are less than the cost increase, the reform reduces placements. I find a negative and economically large effect on placements, implying that the cost of the reform exceeded its private value. Surviving manufactured homes built after 1994 in the highest-wind counties fell by `r cl_count_drop_z3` relative to untreated counties.

The price effect represents net willingness to pay over *all* benefits of the reform. To quantify one source of those benefits, I estimate the effect of the HUD standard on flood damage using claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Although the reform targeted wind damage, the same structural improvements may also improve resilience to flood damage. My identification strategy again exploits variation across housing types and vintages. I compare damages for homes in the same county and two-year construction bin, with county by loss-year fixed effects accounting for local flood conditions. Effectively, the site-built comparison group absorbs secular changes in construction quality and storm severity, isolating any manufactured-home-specific break after 1994. In Zone II and III counties, the pooled estimate indicates roughly `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage per claim and is significant at the 5% level. Event-study and triple-difference estimates are less precise. However, the present value of these benefits is small because the median insured mobile home has a building value of only `r mh_med_value`, `r mh_value_gap_pct` less than the median insured site-built home, and claims are infrequent.

The private benefits of resilience may be reduced by the presence of implicit federal disaster insurance. The federal government insures households against consumption risk from natural disasters both directly, through FEMA disaster relief, and indirectly, through social insurance programs such as Medicaid and SNAP [@deryugina_fiscal_2017]. Consequently, my results do not necessarily imply that the reform was socially inefficient, because fiscal spillovers to the federal budget may be substantial. Among NFIP policyholders in the highest-wind counties, fiscal spillovers (from reduced flood insurance payments) represent `r cl_public_share` of the total estimated flood benefits.

This paper contributes to several literatures. First, it provides direct evidence on the returns to building code regulation for disaster resilience. Prior work on site-built homes exploiting state-level code reforms has found conflicting results [@simmons_economic_2018; @dehring_coastal_2013]. For manufactured housing, my results build on a body of descriptive work examining the 1994 HUD code reform [@simmons_manufactured_2008; @kevin_r_grosskopf_manufactured_2005]. I show that the reform had large effects on the market for mobile homes in treated counties, with quantity declines indicating that buyers valued the additional resilience at less than its cost. I also provide the first causal estimates of the reform's effect on flood damage, market prices, and quantities.

Methodologically, @baylis_mandated_2026 implement a similar study of wildfire building codes in California and find large benefits to mandatory adaptation, with fiscal spillovers and insurance value potentially justifying tighter building codes even in areas with moderate wildfire risk. This paper improves on their empirical strategy by exploiting the federal regulation of manufactured homes, which allows me to separate building code reforms from general vintage effects. Specifically, I compare site-built and manufactured homes within counties and construction-vintage bins, controlling for county by loss-year conditions. My design builds on the set of methodologies used in the economics literature to study building codes, which generally rely on across-vintage or across-location comparisons [@jacobsen_are_2013; @levinson_how_2016].

I also contribute to a rich literature evaluating the fiscal position of the National Flood Insurance Program and the broader fiscal consequences of natural disasters. My results suggest that HUD code reforms had moderate fiscal spillovers on the NFIP through reduced payouts on post-1994 MH claims, and likely additional spillovers on \emph{ex post} disaster relief programs that serve the largely uninsured MH population [@solomon_optimal_2026].

The resale price gap measures the capitalized private value of the reform across benefit channels. I separately quantify flood damage reduction, but do not decompose the remaining valuation into wind damage reduction, reduced displacement, or other benefits. I also do not estimate spillovers to adjacent homes or fiscal spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster assistance.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{institutional-background} describes the institutional background and the 1994 HUD Code reform. Section \ref{empirical-strategy} presents the empirical strategy. Section \ref{data} describes the data. Section \ref{results} reports the results, and Section \ref{conclusion} concludes.

# Institutional Background

## Manufactured Housing and the HUD Code

Approximately 6% of the housing stock consists of manufactured homes. This share is substantially higher in rural areas and in the Southeast, where the share of MH can exceed 15%.[^mh-stats] These homes are disproportionately occupied by low-income households and disproportionately exposed to natural disaster risk. In 1992, Hurricane Andrew destroyed 97% of manufactured homes in its path in Dade County, Florida, compared to 11% of site-built homes.[^florida-case]

[^florida-case]: *Florida Manufactured Housing Ass'n v. Cisneros*, 53 F.3d 1565 (11th Cir. 1995).

[^mh-stats]: Manufactured-Housing Consumer Finance in the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2014. https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/manufactured-housing-consumer-finance-in-the-u-s/. Manufactured homes are built in a factory and transported to a site, as distinct from site-built (stick-built) homes constructed on location.

The vulnerability of manufactured homes to extreme weather prompted a major regulatory response. In 1994, HUD revised the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards---the federal building code governing all manufactured housing---to impose wind resistance requirements. The reform created a three-zone wind classification system and required structural upgrades for homes sited in high-wind zones, including stronger anchoring and strapping, upgraded sheathing and fastening schedules, and wind-pressure requirements for components and cladding. Unlike local building codes for site-built homes, the HUD Code is a federal minimum standard that preempts state and local regulation.

Figure \ref{map:windzone-counties} shows a map of the US counties in each of the three HUD wind zones. Zone III counties, which are subject to the most stringent requirements for winds up to 110 mph, are concentrated in Florida, Louisiana, and North Carolina. Zone II counties, where HUD set requirements for winds up to 100 mph, had less stringent requirements. The vast majority of counties, in Zone I, experienced no change in regulation.

The preemption of local codes is a distinctive feature of the manufactured housing market. Site-built homes are subject to state and local building codes, which vary substantially across jurisdictions and are enforced through local permitting and inspection processes. Manufactured homes, by contrast, must meet a single federal standard set by HUD, which typically inspects units in the factory. This institutional feature is central to the identification strategy, which compares manufactured and site-built homes in the same construction-vintage bin and county, with county by loss-year effects accounting for common flood conditions.

## Flood Insurance for Manufactured Homes

The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) provides federally backed flood insurance to property owners in participating communities. NFIP constitutes the vast majority of flood insurance in the US and uses the Standard Flood Insurance Policy (SFIP), with forms for different property types. For single-family residential properties, coverage limits are $250,000 for the structure and $100,000 for contents.

Historically, flood insurance has been heavily subsidized, with subsidy rates of roughly 50\% [@solomon_optimal_2026]. Flood insurance is mandatory for properties with federally backed mortgages in FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), locations with more than a 1% annual probability of flooding. However, compliance with this mandate is uneven: while over 90% of required homeowners have policies at origination, take-up declines substantially over the lifetime of the mortgage [@us_government_accountability_office_national_2021].

Manufactured homes may be located in trailer parks (where the land is rented) or placed on land owned by the homeowner. Regardless of the land tenure, owners of MH are eligible for the same NFIP policies as site-built homeowners. However, take-up is substantially lower. One reason may be that MH are frequently financed with chattel loans secured only by the unit. Such loans are generally not federally insured and hence not subject to the flood insurance mandate.

The NFIP data used in this paper record claims and policy information at the individual level. This allows direct comparison of flood damage outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes conditional on holding NFIP coverage. Selection into flood insurance coverage is a potential concern, which I address through composition checks on the insured population in Section \ref{selection-and-composition}.

# Empirical Strategy

I first estimate how households value the additional resilience using resale prices. Then, I assess whether the reform reduced surviving manufactured-home quantities. Finally, I quantify one source of benefits, from reduced flood damage, and show how the reform affected the federal flood insurance program.

## Valuations {#valuations}

The 1994 standard raised the wind requirements for manufactured homes built in Zone II and Zone III counties after 1994. Consider a homebuyer choosing between a pre-reform MH and a post-reform MH in a treated county. In equilibrium, the difference in market prices between the two homes reflects the buyer's willingness to pay for the additional resilience provided by the reform. Otherwise, one of the housing types would not transact, because the other would strictly dominate it. The price gap does *not* measure the cost of the reform, which affects all mobile home prices in treated counties by shifting the housing supply curve.

I estimate valuation for resilience by comparing the sales prices of manufactured homes of different construction years across counties in different wind zones. The identifying assumption is that the profile of MH prices across construction vintages would have been the same across wind zones absent the reform.

Vintage profiles may differ across counties because of different depreciation rates (perhaps from climate factors or variation in the price of housing maintenance) or different demand for homes of different vintages (perhaps from changes in household preferences or credit conditions). These factors should not, however, vary systematically across wind zones.

Let $c$ index counties, $s(c)$ denote the state of county $c$, $\nu$ denote the original construction year, and $t$ denote the sale year. Let $Z^{II}_c$ and $Z^{III}_c$ indicate that county $c$ is in Zone II or Zone III.

For a sale $i$ of a manufactured home, the price event study is

\begin{equation}
\ln P_i = \alpha_{c(i),t(i)} + \lambda_{s(c(i)),\nu_i} + \sum_{k \neq 1993} \left( \beta^{II}_k Z^{II}_{c(i)} + \beta^{III}_k Z^{III}_{c(i)} \right) \mathbf{1}[\nu_i = k] + X_i\beta + \varepsilon_i,
\label{eq:es-cost-price}
\end{equation}

where $P_i$ is the real sale price, $\alpha_{c,t}$ is a county $\times$ sale-year fixed effect, $\lambda_{s(c),\nu}$ is a state $\times$ construction-year fixed effect, and $X_i$ is a vector of covariates. The county $\times$ sale-year effect absorbs local housing-market conditions at the time of sale. The state $\times$ construction-year effect allows each state its own vintage profile of manufactured-home prices, so the identifying variation comes from within-state comparisons across counties. I allow $X_i$ to include log living area and log lot size. These controls improve precision in some specifications, but they may be outcomes that themselves respond to the reform, so I exclude them from the main specification.

The two coefficients of interest are $\beta^{II}_k$ and $\beta^{III}_k$. These are the differences in log price between Zone II (III) and Zone I counties for manufactured homes built in year $k$, relative to the same difference for homes built in 1993. I restrict the sample to sales of homes built from `r cl_p_y0` through `r cl_p_y1` that occur in `r cl_sale_y0` or later. The sale window begins after the last construction vintage, so every transaction occurs after the home's construction year. The estimates therefore compare prices of existing homes rather than prices at initial placement.

In static specifications, I replace the zone by construction-year interactions with zone by post-reform interactions, where $\mathrm{Post}_{\nu}=\mathbf{1}[\nu\geq1994]$. Construction year 1994 is therefore included in the post-reform group despite the July effective date.

I also estimate a triple-difference design that compares the vintage price profile against site-built homes in the same counties. This design accounts for local variation in building quality that may affect how prices evolve across vintages. For instance, if Hurricane Andrew caused builders in Zone III counties to improve the quality of all homes built after 1992, or changed beliefs about the likelihood of hurricane damage, then prices of site-built homes would also rise relative to Zone I. Differencing out site-built prices isolates how much of the price increase is specific to manufactured homes.

Let $m \in \{\text{MH}, \text{SB}\}$ denote housing type and let $\text{MH}_i$ indicate a manufactured home. The triple-difference specification is

\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\ln P_i = {} & \alpha_{c(i),t(i),m(i)} + \lambda_{m(i),\nu_i} + \phi^{II} \, \text{Post}_{\nu_i} Z^{II}_{c(i)} + \phi^{III} \, \text{Post}_{\nu_i} Z^{III}_{c(i)} \\
& + \theta^{II} \, \text{Post}_{\nu_i} \text{MH}_i Z^{II}_{c(i)} + \theta^{III} \, \text{Post}_{\nu_i} \text{MH}_i Z^{III}_{c(i)} + \varepsilon_i,
\end{split}
\label{eq:ddd-cost}
\end{equation}

where $\alpha_{c,t,m}$ is a county $\times$ sale-year $\times$ housing-type fixed effect and $\lambda_{m,\nu}$ is a housing-type $\times$ construction-year fixed effect. The coefficient $\phi^{III}$ is the post-1994 change in the log price of site-built homes in Zone III counties, relative to the same change in Zone I counties. The coefficient $\theta^{III}$ is the additional post-1994 change for manufactured homes.

## Quantities {#quantities}

The quantity of newly placed manufactured homes is a sufficient statistic for the net private benefit of the reform. If the reform's benefits exceed its costs, then the quantity of new homes placed in treated counties should be at least as high as it would have been absent the reform. A decline in quantities indicates that homebuyers valued the reform by less than its cost.

One threat to this analysis is that Hurricane Andrew -- the disaster that prompted the reform -- may have simultaneously affected the quantity of MH in treated counties through other channels. For instance, Hurricane Andrew may have caused a temporary spike in construction as homeowners replaced their destroyed homes. Alternatively, it may have affected beliefs about the risk of living in a manufactured home in hurricane-prone areas, permanently reducing placements.

I address this concern by setting the omitted category to 1991, the year before Hurricane Andrew, which made landfall in August 1992. Homes built in 1993 and in the first half of 1994 were affected by the hurricane but not by the HUD reform, which took effect in July 1994.

Let $N_{c\nu}$ denote the number of surviving manufactured homes in county $c$ with construction year $\nu$ observed in 2023. The quantity event study is

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{E}[N_{c\nu}] = \exp\left( \alpha_c + \lambda_{s(c),\nu} + \sum_{k \neq 1991} \left( \beta^{II}_k Z^{II}_c + \beta^{III}_k Z^{III}_c \right) \mathbf{1}[\nu = k] \right),
\label{eq:es-cost-quantity}
\end{equation}

where $\alpha_c$ is a county fixed effect and the other variables are as defined above. I estimate Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-quantity} by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood on a panel that contains every construction year for each county in the quantity sample, retaining zero counts. The coefficients are differences in log counts relative to 1991.

The identifying assumption is that, absent the standard, the vintage profile of surviving manufactured-home counts would have been the same across wind zones within a state. In this case, state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects absorb state-specific shocks to the housing market that affected new construction.

One nuance to this analysis is that the quantity measure counts surviving homes, not new placements. If MH built after 1994 are more resilient to hurricanes, and hence less likely to be replaced, their surviving counts will be inflated relative to pre-reform homes. This would bias the estimated effect of the reform upward, toward a smaller decline in surviving homes. Consequently, my finding of a decline is conservative.

I also estimate Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-quantity} with the number of site-built homes as the outcome. This specification serves as a placebo test: did treated counties experience general changes in housing construction after 1994 that affected all housing types, or were the effects specific to manufactured homes? Importantly, any substitution between the two types means that the HUD reform should increase construction of site-built homes, as their attractiveness relative to the newly-costly MH increases, so a small increase in site-built homes is consistent with the reform reducing MH placements.

## Benefits from Reduced Flood Damage {#benefits}

I estimate flood benefits by comparing manufactured and site-built homes in Zone II and III counties. The identifying assumption is that, absent the HUD reform, the proportional vintage profile of expected flood damage would have been the same for both housing types. Let $i$ index a claim made in year $t$ for a home in county $c(i)$ and two-year construction bin $\nu_i$, indexed by its first year. The event study specification is

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{E}[Y_{it} \mid X_{it}] = \exp\left(\alpha_{c(i),t} + \delta_m + \lambda_{\nu_i} + \sum_{k \neq 1991} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\nu_i = k] \times \text{MH}_i)\right)
\label{eq:event-study-benefit}
\end{equation}

where $Y_{it}$ is the outcome in levels (e.g., building damage), $\alpha_{c(i),t}$ is a county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect absorbing location-specific storm severity, $\delta_m$ is a manufactured housing indicator absorbing time-invariant differences between housing types, $\lambda_{\nu_i}$ indicates the construction vintage, and $\text{MH}_i$ is an indicator for manufactured homes.

I estimate the model by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML), retaining zero outcomes and clustering standard errors by county. The coefficients $\beta_k$ capture the manufactured-home-specific proportional vintage profile relative to the omitted construction bin 1992--1993, the last pre-reform bin. A coefficient $b$ corresponds to a proportional change of $\exp(b)-1$ in the conditional mean. I pool construction vintages into two-year bins to improve precision because flood claims for manufactured homes are relatively rare.

Identification relies on a parallel trends assumption in the vintage profile of outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes in the absence of the HUD code reform. In other words, homes built at different times may experience different levels of flood damage due to changes in construction quality, storm severity, or intra-county location, but these vintage effects should be the same proportionally for manufactured and site-built homes. The pre-reform building-damage coefficients are not distinguishable from zero, which provides some support for this assumption. Policy-composition profiles show some pre-reform differences, however, so these checks do not establish parallel vintage trends for every outcome.

I expect the cohort effects to grow with later construction cohorts as compliance rates increase. Because of lags between production and installation, some units with post-1994 installation dates may have been manufactured before the regulation took effect in July 1994.

I use the same construction-bin interactions to examine replacement cost, insurance coverage, elevation, and flood-zone designation among individual NFIP policy terms. These specifications replace county by loss-year fixed effects with county by five-year calendar-period fixed effects. They assess whether the insured population changes across construction vintages in ways that could explain the damage estimates.

# Data

## Property Transactions and the Housing Stock {#data-corelogic}

I measure manufactured home prices and quantities at the county level with property records from CoreLogic. The records consist of two files. The first is a 2023 snapshot of all residential parcels, with each parcel's county, original construction year, land use, and an indicator for whether the parcel contains a manufactured home. The second records deed transfers, with the sale date and price.

I classify a parcel as a manufactured home if the indicator is set. I classify a parcel as site-built if it is recorded as a single-family residence, the indicator is not set, and its land use is not a mobile-home lot or park. Parcels in manufactured-home parks and parcels with multiple buildings or units are excluded. The records therefore cover mainly manufactured homes on land held by the owner of the home.

The price sample consists of arm's-length sales from `r cl_sale_y0` through `r cl_sale_y1` of homes with original construction years `r cl_p_y0` through `r cl_p_y1`. I restrict the sample to arm's-length sales with non-zero prices that are not part of a multi- or split-parcel transaction and are not flagged as foreclosures or short sales. I also exclude cases with multiple transactions on the same day and transactions dated before January 1 of the construction year.

Prices are deflated to 2000 dollars with the CPI-U. The construction window matches the 1988--1999 window used for NFIP claims and policy composition. It ends before the Florida Building Code took effect in March 2002 but does not fully exclude Florida's manufactured-home installation changes effective in 1999. The price sample contains roughly `r cl_n_mh_sales` million sales of manufactured homes and `r cl_n_sb_sales` million sales of site-built homes.

Table \ref{tab:sumstats-corelogic} reports transaction counts and surviving-home counts by housing type and construction vintage. It also reports mean and median manufactured-home transaction prices by wind zone; these prices include land.

The quantity measure counts parcels in the 2023 cross-section by county, construction year, and housing type, regardless of whether they are ever sold. These counts are surviving homes, so a home built in 1990 and destroyed or removed before 2023 is not counted. Each count reflects both the number of homes built and the share that survived to 2023. The static quantity sample contains `r cl_n_mh_homes` manufactured homes and `r cl_n_sb_homes` site-built homes built from `r cl_q_y0` through `r cl_q_y1`, in the `r cl_n_cty_q` counties with at least one manufactured home built in that window.

Each county is assigned its HUD wind zone under 24 CFR \S 3280.305 (Figure \ref{map:windzone-counties}). Zones II and III are treated; Zone I is the control. Every Florida county is in Zone II or Zone III. Outside Florida, the Zone III counties are in Louisiana and North Carolina. I exclude Alaska and Hawaii.

## Flood Damage and Insurance Coverage

I use two FEMA datasets on individual flood insurance claims and policies. Claims data record the date of loss, construction year, building and contents damage amounts, NFIP payments, property characteristics, and the census tract. Policy data record coverage amounts, premium, property characteristics, and flood zone designation.

### Final Sample

I restrict the sample to homes with construction years between 1988 and 1999 and loss years from 1994 through 2023. The construction window ends in 1999, before the Florida Building Code took effect in March 2002. It does not fully exclude Florida's manufactured-home installation changes effective in 1999.[^fl-standards] The baseline claims and policy samples are restricted to HUD wind Zones II and III, where the 1994 reform raised wind requirements. Appendix \ref{appendix-triple-diff} adds Zone I counties as a further comparison group. I further restrict both the claims and policy data to detached single-family residential properties, using the occupancy classification recorded in each dataset; this excludes multi-unit residential buildings and non-residential structures from the site-built comparison group.

Insurance claims and policies for manufactured homes are relatively rare, so the event studies bin construction years into two-year periods: 1988--1989, 1990--1991, 1992--1993, 1994--1995, 1996--1997, and 1998--1999. The construction-year window is chosen so that 1992--1993 is the last pre-reform bin and every bin contains two full construction years.

[^fl-standards]: Florida's official rule history dates the anchoring and tie-down amendment (Fla. Admin. Code r. 15C-1.0104, ``Installation Standards for Anchors and Tie-downs'') to March 31, 1999. Ending the construction sample in 1999 therefore does not fully exclude this installation change. \url{https://flrules.org/gateway/ruleno.asp?Section=0&id=15C-1.0104}

I identify manufactured homes using the NFIP floor-count code for mobile homes. The site-built comparison group consists of homes with one to three floors. Claims with negative net building or contents payments are excluded from the estimation sample so that the PPML outcomes are nonnegative.

Policy records are available only beginning in 2009, so the policy panel spans three five-year calendar periods: 2009--2013, 2014--2018, and 2019--2023. The policy-composition regressions use the same construction-vintage window and single-family residential occupancy classification as the claims data. Descriptive policy rates and take-up calculations instead use 1984--1999 construction vintages, matching the available Census-anchored stock denominator.

All nominal values are deflated to constant (2000) dollars using the CPI-U. I restrict both samples to the continental US. Table \ref{tab:sumstats-nfip} reports summary statistics for the NFIP data by construction vintage and housing type. Manufactured homes generally experience lower building and contents damage than site-built homes, with correspondingly lower coverage amounts. I observe `r n_mh_claims` claims for manufactured homes in the sample, or roughly `r mh_claim_pct`% of all claims. This share is substantially lower than the share of manufactured homes in the overall housing stock \citep{genz_why_2001}.

# Results {#results}

## Evidence of a resale price premium {#valuation-results}

Figure \ref{fig:es-cost-price} plots the coefficients $\beta^{II}_k$ and $\beta^{III}_k$ of Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-price} with state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects. Prices of homes built before the reform are similar across treated and untreated counties. After 1994, I find suggestive evidence that prices increased, with larger effects in Zone III counties, though individual point estimates are imprecise.

Table \ref{tab:cost-static} reports the static price estimates under various specifications. The first three columns report difference-in-differences estimates, adding state-by-vintage and size controls progressively. The Zone III point estimates are positive but not generally significant at conventional levels. The Zone II estimates are close to zero.

The last three columns report the triple-difference estimates. These models suggest that site-built home prices also changed after 1994 in treated counties. The additional change for MH in Zone III is positive but not generally significant at conventional levels.

All price specifications require positive, finite living area and lot size. Columns (1)--(3) use the same retained MH observations, and columns (4)--(6) use the same retained MH and site-built observations; adding size controls therefore does not change the sample.

Let $\hat b^{III}$ denote the Zone III coefficient for manufactured homes in each specification. To express these log-price estimates in dollars, I multiply $\exp(\hat b^{III})-1$ by the mean transaction price of Zone III manufactured homes built in `r cl_p_y0`--1993, which is `r cl_price_base` in 2000 dollars. The baseline estimate, column (2), implies a premium of `r cl_premium`; across the four specifications without size controls, the dollar equivalents range from `r cl_premium_lo` to `r cl_premium_hi`.

## Quantities of surviving manufactured homes fell after the reform {#quantity-results}

Figure \ref{fig:es-cost-quantity} plots the coefficients of Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-quantity} for surviving manufactured homes.

The pre-Andrew quantity coefficients do not show a clear monotonic differential trend, although the 1987 Zone III coefficient is positive and individually significant. After 1992, I find an economically small and imprecise increase in placements in both Zone II and Zone III counties, consistent with either replacement of homes destroyed by Hurricane Andrew or anticipation of the HUD code reform. After 1994, surviving MH in Zone III counties decline sharply, with large negative coefficients from 1995 through 1999. The timing is consistent with regulation rather than with changes in beliefs or rebuilding caused by Hurricane Andrew. Estimates for Zone II are imprecise but suggest a smaller negative effect.

Table \ref{tab:cost-static-quantity} reports static count estimates. Columns (1) and (2) use manufactured homes as the outcome. The Zone III effects are `r lad_pc("count", 1, 3)` and `r lad_pc("count", 2, 3)`.

Columns (3) and (4) repeat these specifications using site-built homes as the outcome. With state $\times$ vintage effects, I find no evidence that site-built housing quantities changed significantly after 1994. The Zone III point estimate is negative and imprecise, so these estimates do not establish substitution toward site-built housing.

The counts measure homes that survived to 2023, so a change in the count combines a change in the number of homes placed and a change in the share that survived. Two forces are expected to raise the survival of post-1994 homes in Zone II and Zone III counties relative to pre-1994 homes: the pre-1994 homes were built to the weaker standard, and they have been exposed to hurricanes for more years. Both forces raise the post-1994 count relative to the pre-1994 count, so they bias the estimate against finding a decline.

I replicate these results using counts of housing units from the 2000 decennial Census (Appendix \ref{appendix-census}). The quantity effects are consistent with CoreLogic, and indicate that the declines in manufactured homes are not artifacts of the CoreLogic data or of the use of parcels surviving to 2023.

## Benefit Side: Flood Damage

I first report effects on damage and NFIP payments conditional on a claim. I then assess changes in the composition of insured homes. The baseline estimates use Zone II and III counties; the appendix adds Zone I as a comparison group.

### Evidence of reduced flood damage

Figure \ref{fig:es-building-damage} presents the event study for building damage per claim. The two pre-1994 coefficients are small and indistinguishable from zero. Beginning with the 1994 construction cohort, manufactured homes experience lower building damage relative to site-built homes, averaging `r bldg_dmg_evt_avg` across the two post-reform construction bins (1994--1996 and 1997--1999). Both post-reform building-damage coefficients are negative but imprecisely estimated; the later bin has a smaller reduction.

Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static} collapses this vintage profile to a single pre- and post-1994 comparison. Manufactured homes built after 1994 experience a `r bldg_dmg_pct` reduction in building damage per claim relative to the change for site-built homes of the same vintage (coefficient `r bldg_dmg_lp`, standard error `r bldg_dmg_se`). The estimate is significant at the 5% level, with a 95% confidence interval corresponding to reductions of approximately `r bldg_dmg_reduction_ci_lo` to `r bldg_dmg_reduction_ci_hi`. Applied to the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean of `r mh_pre_bldg` per claim, this is a reduction of `r bldg_dmg_eff`. Net building payments also decline. The contents-damage point estimate is smaller and imprecise. Net contents payments show a larger but less precise decline.

Appendix \ref{appendix-triple-diff} adds counties in wind Zone I as a further comparison group, which provides a triple-difference robustness check analogous to the supplementary price specification. The post-1994 reduction in building damage is largest in Zone III and smallest in Zone I, though point estimates are imprecise.

To express flood benefits per insured home, I apply the zone-specific proportional damage and payment estimates to pre-1994 manufactured-home mean losses, multiply by the insured claim rate for the baseline vintage groups in the same wind zone, and discount the resulting annual savings at `r hud_rate` over `r hud_life` years. The claim-rate denominator uses Census-compatible vintage groups, with the mixed 1990--1994 group assigned to the baseline. This calculation holds claim frequency fixed and assumes that the proportional reductions apply to the baseline mean losses. In Zone III, avoided building and contents damage has a present value of `r cl_flood_pv` per insured home. Of this, `r cl_public_pv` is reduced NFIP payments, leaving `r cl_retained_pv` in losses avoided by the insured household. These amounts measure the flood channel; the resale price premium captures the capitalized private value of resilience across channels.

## Composition changes {#selection-and-composition}

I next assess whether the revised wind standards affected the composition of flood insurance policyholders. Such changes in composition might arise if resilience and insurance are substitutes, so that the reform caused some households to drop coverage. Conversely, the reform may have increased insurance take-up if insurers perceived post-1994 MH as less risky and offered those households lower premiums.

Table \ref{tab:composition} reports event studies for five policy characteristics: replacement cost, building coverage, contents coverage, and indicators for whether the home is elevated or in a Special Flood Hazard Area.

All five outcomes are estimated by PPML and are therefore on the same log-point scale.

Averaging the two post-reform log coefficients with equal weights and converting the averages to percentages, replacement cost and building coverage increase for manufactured homes relative to site-built homes by `r comp_repl_avg_pct` and `r comp_bldg_avg_pct`, respectively. Post-reform MH are generally of higher quality than those built before, which suggests that their exposure to flood risk, and hence average claim amount, should be higher rather than lower. This shift works against the estimated decline. Likewise, I estimate that post-reform MH are more likely to be located in a Special Flood Hazard Area, which again raises expected flood damage. Contents coverage shows no significant post-reform shift. Elevation shows no clear post-reform change: both point estimates are small, negative, and imprecise. Some pre-reform differences in replacement cost and coverage limit the causal interpretation of these composition profiles.

# Conclusion

The 1994 HUD wind standard likely reduced welfare for households that wanted to purchase mobile homes in hurricane-prone locations. The price estimates suggest a positive but imprecisely estimated valuation of the reform. Surviving quantities declined substantially, indicating that the private benefits of resilience were less than the cost increase.

For the 22 million Americans living in manufactured homes---disproportionately low-income, credit-constrained, and underinsured---these findings point to limited gains from mandatory adaptation for low-value assets. Manufactured homes represent an alternative climate adaptation strategy: households tie up fewer assets in high-risk locations by purchasing a cheap, easy-to-replace home.

The remaining case for the efficiency of the HUD wind reform is fiscal: disaster relief transfers part of the benefit of resilience from owners to the government. Before implementing the new standard, HUD forecast that federal relief would decrease by `r cl_hud_public` per home in Zone III. Subject to this caveat, the results indicate that the 1994 standard cost buyers of manufactured homes more than they valued it and that the flood benefits it produced are small in dollars.

\appendix

# NFIP Take-Up: Stock Construction {#appendix-take-up}

The take-up calculations underlying Table \ref{tab:sumstats-nfip} divide policy counts by an imputed stock of homes of the same county, construction vintage, and housing type. Raw policy counts alone combine insurance participation with the number of homes available to insure.

## Stock construction

Census 2000 provides occupied housing-unit counts by county, broad construction-vintage bin, and structure type. I use mobile homes for the manufactured-home stock and one-unit attached or detached structures for the single-family comparison stock. Multifamily units and boats, recreational vehicles, and vans are excluded. To include vacant homes, I multiply each occupied vintage count by the ratio of all housing units to occupied housing units for the same county and structure type, calculated across all vintages. This adjustment assumes that the vacancy rate does not vary by vintage within a county and housing type. County-types with no occupied units have no observed vintage distribution and do not receive an imputed vintage stock.

Within each Census vintage bin, I allocate manufactured homes across construction years in proportion to state-year placements from the Survey of Manufactured Housing. Counties within a state receive the same annual shares. I allocate single-family homes using county-year single-family building permits, falling back to state shares when a county has no recorded permits in a bin. If the annual source provides no usable allocation, the bin is split equally across its years. These sources determine annual shares, not stock levels. A proportional undercount constant across a bin's years cancels from those shares; year-specific changes in coverage do not.

Shares are normalized over the full Census bin before restricting the construction window to 1984--1999. Thus, 1984--1989 receives only its allocated share of the 1980--1989 stock. Construction year 1994 is retained and coded as post-reform, although the July effective date makes it a mixture of pre- and post-reform homes. The final Census bin covers 1999 through March 2000; the allocation gives 2000 a three-month weight and retains only the 1999 stock.

## Counts, exposures, and specification

The sampling frame crosses every positive-stock county, vintage, and housing-type cell with the three five-year calendar periods covering 2009--2023. I attach observed policy and claim counts to this frame and set absent counts to zero. Stock is counted once per county and vintage, regardless of how many tracts report policies. Claims are counted directly from the claims sample, including locations with no observed policies. Cells with zero policies remain in the policies-per-home and claims-per-home regressions. Claims per policy requires positive policy exposure. Poisson estimation additionally removes fixed-effect groups with an outcome of zero throughout.

Home-years equal the imputed 2000 stock multiplied by the five calendar years in a period. Policy-years count policy terms. Each regression includes the logarithm of its exposure as an offset. The specification includes county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effects, a housing-type fixed effect, a post-1994 main effect, and a post-1994 $\times$ manufactured-home interaction, as in the static claims specification. No county $\times$ housing-type fixed effects are added. Standard errors are clustered by state because the annual manufactured-home allocation is shared by counties within a state.

In cells with positive policy counts, claims per home equals policies per home times claims per policy. This identity does not imply that the three fitted coefficients add: the regressions use different exposures and, where exposure is zero, different estimation samples.

## Mandatory and non-mandatory purchase

The mandatory-purchase component has a static coefficient of `r tk_mand_stc` (standard error `r tk_mand_stc_se`), compared with `r tk_nonmand_stc` (standard error `r tk_nonmand_stc_se`) for the non-mandated component. Mandated policies represent `r tk_mand_share` of pre-1994 manufactured-home policy-years. This split describes policies flagged by insurers as mandatory purchases; it does not isolate the building standard from contemporaneous changes in insurance-purchase enforcement, and incomplete reporting of the flag limits its interpretation.

## Stock timing

The denominator is a 2000 snapshot, while policy periods run from 2009 to 2023. Differential demolition, relocation, or changes in vacancy by construction vintage and housing type can make the later stock differ systematically from the imputation. State clustering allows correlated sampling error but does not correct such bias or uncertainty about the vacancy assumption. The estimates therefore describe insurance participation relative to a Census-anchored approximation of the stock, rather than a directly observed annual take-up rate.

# Wind-Zone Triple Difference {#appendix-triple-diff}

The 1994 standard raised wind-resistance requirements only for manufactured homes sited in HUD wind Zones II and III. Manufactured homes built after 1994 for Zone I counties were built to an unchanged standard. A post-1994 change in the manufactured-home damage gap that occurs in Zone I counties is therefore not caused by the wind standard. I use Zone I counties as a comparison group in a triple difference:

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{E}[Y_{it} \mid X_{it}] = \exp\left(\alpha_{c(i),t} + \delta_{m,T_{c(i)}} + \lambda_{P_i,T_{c(i)}} + \beta \, (P_i \times \text{MH}_i) + \gamma \, (P_i \times \text{MH}_i \times T_{c(i)})\right)
\label{eq:triple-diff}
\end{equation}

where $P_i = \mathbf{1}[\nu_i \geq 1994]$, $T_c$ indicates that county $c$ is in wind Zone II or III, $\delta_{m,T}$ is a housing-type effect specific to treatment status, and $\lambda_{P,T}$ is a post-1994 effect common to both housing types and specific to treatment status. The county $\times$ loss-year effect $\alpha_{c(i),t}$ absorbs the main effect of $T_c$. The coefficient $\beta$ is the post-1994 change in the manufactured-home damage gap in Zone I counties. The coefficient $\gamma$ is the additional change in Zone II and III counties. $\gamma$ identifies the effect of the standard if, absent the reform, the post-1994 change in the gap would have been the same in Zone I counties and in Zone II and III counties. Unlike the baseline, this design allows a common manufactured-home-specific post-1994 shift across treated and untreated zones. The identifying comparison is proportional, as in the baseline PPML model. A second specification replaces $T_c$ with separate indicators for Zone II and Zone III, with housing-type and post-1994 effects specific to each zone.

Table \ref{tab:windzone-ddd-building} reports the estimates for building damage. Column (1) is the baseline estimate of Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static}. Zone I counties account for `r wz_mh_z1_shr` of manufactured-home claims. In column (2), the post-1994 change in Zone I is `r wz_did_z1` (SE `r wz_did_z1_se`) and the additional change in Zones II and III is `r wz_ddd_tr` (SE `r wz_ddd_tr_se`). In column (3), the additional change is `r wz_ddd_z2` (SE `r wz_ddd_z2_se`) in Zone II and `r wz_ddd_z3` (SE `r wz_ddd_z3_se`) in Zone III. Equivalently, the post-1994 change in the gap is `r wz_did_z1` in Zone I, `r wz_did_z2` in Zone II, and `r wz_did_z3` in Zone III. The reduction is ordered by the stringency of the wind requirement, and the Zone I change is not distinguishable from zero. The additional wind-zone contrasts are imprecise, so the ordered point estimates do not establish statistically distinct effects across zones. Zone III comprises `r wz_n_cty_z3` counties in `r wz_n_state_z3` states. Standard errors are clustered by county, the level at which wind zones are assigned.

# Census 2000 Counts of Manufactured Homes {#appendix-census}

This appendix repeats the quantity design of Section \ref{quantity-results} with Census 2000 counts of occupied housing units. The outcome is the number of occupied manufactured homes in a county built in a given vintage bin. The bins are 1980--1989, 1990--1994, 1995--1998, and 1999--2000 (through March), and 1990--1994 is the reference bin. Post-reform bins are 1995--1998 and 1999--2000. Census bins do not separate 1994 into pre- and post-reform homes, so the 1990--1994 bin is treated as pre-reform. The sample contains `r cen_n_counties` counties with at least one manufactured home in the four bins; Alaska and Hawaii are excluded. Counties absent from the wind-zone list are assigned to Zone I. As a comparison group, I use occupied one-unit site-built homes in the same bins.

Let $y_{cb}$ be the count of occupied manufactured homes in county $c$ and bin $b$. I estimate by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood
\begin{equation}
  y_{cb} = \exp\left(\alpha_c + \gamma_{s(c),b} + \theta^{II} Z^{II}_c \times \text{Post}_b + \theta^{III} Z^{III}_c \times \text{Post}_b\right) \varepsilon_{cb},
\end{equation}
where $Z^{II}_c$ and $Z^{III}_c$ indicate Zone II and Zone III counties, $\text{Post}_b$ indicates the post-reform bins, $\alpha_c$ is a county effect, and $\gamma_{s(c),b}$ is a state $\times$ bin effect. Column (1) replaces $\gamma_{s(c),b}$ with a common bin effect. Columns (3) and (4) use the same two specifications with occupied one-unit site-built homes as the outcome. Columns (5) and (6) use the specification of column (2) for owner-occupied and renter-occupied manufactured homes, respectively. Standard errors are clustered by county. Table \ref{tab:census-static} reports the estimates.

With state $\times$ bin effects in column (2), occupied manufactured homes built in 1995--2000 fall by `r cen_ppc(2, 3)` in Zone III counties (`r cen_pb(2, 3)`, standard error `r cen_pse(2, 3)`) and by `r cen_ppc(2, 2)` in Zone II counties (`r cen_pb(2, 2)`, standard error `r cen_pse(2, 2)`), relative to Zone I counties and to the 1990--1994 bin. With common bin effects in column (1), the Zone III estimate is `r cen_pb(1, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(1, 3)`). Site-built homes also decline in the Census counts with common bin effects: `r cen_pb(3, 2)` in Zone II (standard error `r cen_pse(3, 2)`) and `r cen_pb(3, 3)` in Zone III (standard error `r cen_pse(3, 3)`) in column (3). With state $\times$ bin effects in column (4), they are `r cen_pb(4, 2)` (standard error `r cen_pse(4, 2)`) and `r cen_pb(4, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(4, 3)`), and neither is distinguishable from zero at the 5% level in Zone II or Zone III. In both zones, the manufactured-home estimates are larger in magnitude than the site-built estimates. The signs and the ordering of Zone III below Zone II are the same as in the CoreLogic estimates in Table \ref{tab:cost-static-quantity}.

The decline in the Zone III count is concentrated among owner-occupied homes. The column (5) estimate is `r cen_pb(5, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(5, 3)`) for owner-occupied manufactured homes, and the column (6) estimate is `r cen_pb(6, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(6, 3)`) for renter-occupied homes, which is not distinguishable from zero. In Zone II the two estimates are similar, `r cen_pb(5, 2)` (standard error `r cen_pse(5, 2)`) and `r cen_pb(6, 2)` (standard error `r cen_pse(6, 2)`).

The Census counts differ from the CoreLogic counts in three ways. They record occupied homes in 2000 rather than parcels observed in 2023, so they are measured closer to the time of placement and are less affected by later survival. They include homes on rented sites, which may not appear as parcels with a manufactured home in property records. The post-reform window is two bins, 1995--2000, and the final bin is short. These differences make the Census estimates a check on the direction and rough size of the CoreLogic quantity decline, not a replication on the same sample.

Two alternative samples give similar Zone III estimates in column (2): excluding Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties, where Hurricane Andrew struck in 1992 (`r cen_b("noandrew", 2, 3)`), and adjusting counts for vacancy (`r cen_b("vacadj", 2, 3)`).

# State-Level Estimates from the Manufactured Housing Survey {#appendix-mhs}

This appendix reports a state-level design for the price and quantity effects of the 1994 standard. It assigns treatment by state rather than by county: a state is treated if it contains any county in wind Zone II or III, and all other states are controls. A treated state can include Zone I counties, in which the standard did not bind. Appendix \ref{appendix-windzone-intensity} reports the share of each treated state's manufactured-home stock that is sited in Zone II or III counties.

## Data and Price Index

This appendix estimates price and quantity effects from a state-by-year panel from the Census Bureau's Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS), which reports average sales prices and placement counts by state. The sample covers 1988--2004. It extends ten years past the reform so that it spans both the expansion of chattel lending for manufactured homes in the late 1990s and the contraction of that lending after 1999. The treatment group consists of states containing HUD wind zones II or III; the control group is zone I states.

Manufactured homes are placed in two sizes. A single-section home arrives as one transportable unit; a multi-section home arrives as two or more units that are joined on site. Multi-section homes are larger and more expensive: over the sample period the average real sales price is `r avg_p_single` for a single-section home and `r avg_p_double` for a multi-section home, a ratio of `r price_ratio` to one. The survey reports an average sales price for each size separately and an average across all homes placed. The all-homes average is the placement-weighted mixture of the two size-specific averages, so it rises both when prices rise and when placements shift toward multi-section homes. The multi-section share differs across states and changes over the sample period, so the all-homes average conflates price changes with changes in the size mix, and a shift in the mix would enter a difference-in-differences estimate as a price effect.

I therefore construct a fixed-weight price index. Let $p^{S}_{st}$ and $p^{D}_{st}$ denote the average real sales price of single-section and multi-section homes in state $s$ and year $t$. The index is

\begin{equation}
P_{st} = \omega^{S} p^{S}_{st} + \omega^{D} p^{D}_{st},
\label{eq:price-index}
\end{equation}

where $\omega^{S}$ and $\omega^{D}$ are the shares of single- and multi-section homes among all homes placed nationally between 1988 and 1993, the six years preceding the reform. These weights are `r wt_single` and `r wt_double`, and they are held fixed across all states and all years. The index is therefore the cost of a fixed basket of homes: it changes only when the price of a size changes, and by construction no variation in the size mix, either across states or over time, can enter it. I report the index normalized so that its national 1993 value equals 100. The normalization divides the index by the single constant `r idx_base`, so the normalized and dollar-denominated versions of the index give the same estimates in different units.

Constructing the index requires both size-specific averages. The survey suppresses these for states with few placements, so the index is defined for `r n_index` of the `r n_raw` state-years in which the all-homes average is published. The excluded state-years are small states, predominantly in the control group. The quantity analysis uses these same state-years, even though placement counts are published more widely, so that the price and quantity effects are estimated on one sample and can be read together. All specifications are weighted by the state's average number of shipments between 1988 and 1993; `r n_dropped_mhs` states with no recorded shipments over that period are dropped from the sample.

## Specification

I estimate the effect of the 1994 HUD standard on manufactured home prices using a two-way fixed effects event study:

\begin{equation}
P_{st} = \alpha_s + \gamma_t + \sum_{k \neq 1993} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\text{year} = k] \times \text{Treated}_s) + \varepsilon_{st}
\label{eq:event-study-cost}
\end{equation}

where $P_{st}$ is the fixed-weight price index of Equation \eqref{eq:price-index} for state $s$ in year $t$, $\alpha_s$ and $\gamma_t$ are state and year fixed effects, and $\text{Treated}_s$ indicates states containing wind zones II or III. The 1993 interaction is omitted: with state fixed effects the full set of treated-by-year interactions is collinear with the time-invariant treated indicator. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore trace out the price difference between treated and control states relative to 1993. All MHS specifications, including this one, are weighted by the state's average number of shipments between 1988 and 1993. Standard errors are clustered by state.

## Results

Figure \ref{fig:es-price} presents the event study for the fixed-weight manufactured home price index. Prior to 1994, treated and control states follow parallel trends: the pre-treatment coefficients are small, precisely estimated, and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The index diverges after 1993, separates fully from 1995 onward, and rises through 1999. These are also the years of a rapid expansion of chattel lending for manufactured homes, which ended in 1999. Placements in treated states rise relative to control states over the same years and fall below them afterward (Figure \ref{fig:es-placements}), which is the pattern a regional expansion and contraction of credit would produce. Part of the price gap during the late 1990s may therefore reflect credit-driven demand rather than the cost of compliance.

The gap narrows after 1999 but remains positive through 2004. The average of the 2000--2004 coefficients is `r price_eff`, corresponding to `r price_pct` of the pre-reform index level of `r avg_price_tr` in treated states. Persistence beyond the lending expansion does not establish that the remaining gap measures compliance costs: regional credit conditions, repossession supply, and demand can have lasting effects. The main text therefore uses county-level wind-zone comparisons and treats these state-level estimates as supplementary evidence.

The 1994 coefficient is small relative to those that follow, and the separation appears from 1995. This is what the timing of the reform implies: the standard took effect in July 1994, so only part of that year's placements were subject to it, and lags between production and installation push further compliance into 1995. The premium persists through 2004, but its source---higher production costs, quality upgrading, regional credit conditions, or demand-side valuation---is not pinned down by the price path alone.

Because the outcome holds the size mix fixed, this estimate cannot reflect a shift in the composition of placements toward more expensive multi-section homes. Two comparisons show how much that restriction matters. First, holding the sample fixed, the all-homes average sales price yields `r price_eff_raw_cmn` against the index's `r price_eff`; valuing each state-year's actual size mix at fixed national prices, so that the mix shift is the only source of variation, yields `r price_eff_comp`, and the treated-control difference in the multi-section share after 1994 is `r share_dbl_eff` percentage points. The size mix therefore accounts for almost none of the price effect. Second, estimated on every state-year for which it is published rather than only those where the index is defined, the all-homes average yields `r price_eff_raw`. The gap between that figure and the index estimate is driven by the small states that drop out when both size-specific prices are required, not by composition.

I also find that price effects are larger for multi-section units (`r price_eff_double`) than for single-section units (`r price_eff_single`), though differential exposure to credit and demand shifts can also generate this pattern (Table \ref{tab:mhs-section-type}).

HUD's prospective analysis provides a benchmark for these price effects. As reproduced in \citet[Table 4-17]{dacquisto_housing_2006}, the analysis predicted consumer price increases of \$829 and \$1,007 for single- and multi-section homes in Zone II, and \$1,177 and \$1,512 in Zone III, using a 56\% pass-through rate. These figures use the analysis's 1992 price baseline, whereas the estimates here are in 2000 dollars. An alternative with nearly full pass-through predicts increases ranging from \$1,402 to \$2,695. Comparing these forecasts with the estimated price response requires a common dollar year and weights for home size and wind-zone exposure. Such a comparison evaluates the joint predictions of accounting-based compliance costs and assumed pass-through; a discrepancy alone cannot identify which component accounts for it.

Figure \ref{fig:es-placements} shows the corresponding event study for log placements, estimated on the same state-years as the price index so that the price and quantity effects describe one panel rather than two. Collapsing the post-period to a single coefficient gives `r plc_eff` log points (SE `r plc_se`), a 95% interval of `r plc_ci_lo` to `r plc_ci_hi`. The point estimate is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The single coefficient averages over two phases: placements in treated states rise relative to control states through 1998 and fall below them after 1999, following the expansion and contraction of chattel lending described above. The interval is wide enough to contain declines of roughly `r fmt_lp(abs(get_mhs("placements_effect_static") - 1.96 * get_mhs("placements_effect_static_se")))` log points as well as increases, so a modest decline cannot be ruled out. These state-level estimates do not distinguish valuation of improved construction from changes in credit supply or other demand shifts.

# Price Effects by Home Size {#appendix-section-type}

The fixed-weight index of Equation \eqref{eq:price-index} removes variation in the size mix by valuing a single national basket, but it does not report whether the reform raised the price of single-section and multi-section homes by the same amount. Table \ref{tab:mhs-section-type} answers that question directly. I stack the panel so that each observation is one state, year, and home size, and I estimate the single-coefficient version of Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-cost} with size-specific state and year fixed effects. Identification is therefore within home size, and the size mix cannot enter the estimate for the same reason it cannot enter the index. Observations are weighted by each state's mean 1988--1993 placements (the same base-period weight used throughout Appendix \ref{appendix-mhs}) times the national base-period share of their size, which reproduces the fixed-weight index where both size-specific prices are published and additionally retains the state-years where only one of the two is published.

Column (1) pools the two sizes and yields an estimate close to the static fixed-weight index estimate, while additionally retaining state-years with only one published size-specific price. Column (2) interacts the post-1994 treatment indicator with home size. Estimating the same contrast on each size separately, on that size's observations alone and with its own state and year fixed effects, gives identical coefficients, so the interaction is not an artifact of the shared fixed effects. The estimated effect for multi-section homes is about 45% larger than for single-section homes. Two readings are consistent with this pattern and the data here do not separate them: compliance may require more material on a larger structure, so that part of the cost scales with size, or multi-section homes may be placed disproportionately in the higher wind zones within treated states, where the binding requirements are stricter.

# Wind-Zone Treatment Intensity by State {#appendix-windzone-intensity}

The binary treatment indicator used in Appendix \ref{appendix-mhs} codes a state as treated if it contains any Zone II or III county, regardless of how much of the state's manufactured housing stock actually sits in one. This is a coarse proxy: a state can be classified treated on the strength of a single high-wind county while the bulk of its MH stock sits in Zone I. Table \ref{tab:windzone-intensity} reports, for every state with at least one Zone II/III county, the share of its 1980--2000 manufactured-housing stock located in a Zone II/III county, constructed by weighting each county's wind-zone status (24 CFR \S 3280.305, as classified in the eCFR crosswalk) by its manufactured-housing stock from the 2000 Census. Only 3 of the 11 treated states---Florida, Louisiana, and Massachusetts---have more than half of their MH stock in a Zone II/III county; pooling across all treated states, only about 30\% of the 1980--2000 MH stock sits in a Zone II/III county.
